notes.8:2: The Vulgate reads super portam Ulai ("by/over the gate of Ulai") here and ante portam ("before the gate") in 8:6, as well as ante paludem ("before the marsh") in 8:3, where the Hebrew has "canal/stream" (uval).
notes.8:9: The Vulgate translates Hebrew "the glorious [land]" here and "the host" in 8:10-13 consistently with fortitudo ("strength"); in 8:12 it renders "host" with robur ("power").
notes.8:13: Latin alteri nescio cui ("to another, I do not know whom") is Jerome's idiomatic rendering of the rare Hebrew term palmoni ("a certain one").
notes.8:16: The Clementine Vulgate reads feminine istam visionem ("this vision") without an explicit personal object, whereas the Hebrew reads "make this man understand the vision."
notes.8:25: Latin in copia rerum omnium ("in the abundance of all things") is a distinctly Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew phrase meaning "without warning" or "in security."
notes.9:23: Latin vir desideriorum ("a man of desires") translates Hebrew ish chamudot ("greatly beloved" or "precious man") literally.
notes.9:24: The Vulgate reads abbreviatae sunt ("have been shortened") where the Hebrew verb is commonly rendered "decreed," and masculine capitalized Sanctus sanctorum ("the Holy One of holies") rather than a neuter "most holy place."
notes.9:25: Latin christum ducem ("Christ the leader") renders Hebrew mashiach nagid ("anointed leader/prince") with christus ("anointed one/Christ") and joins the seven and sixty-two weeks as a single span.
notes.9:26: The Vulgate reads et non erit ejus populus qui eum negaturus est ("and the people who will deny Him will not be His"), where the Hebrew reads "and shall have nothing," and concludes with vastitas ("devastation") and post finem belli ("after the end of the war").
notes.9:27: The Vulgate uses intransitive deficiet ("will cease/fail") rather than a causative verb and reads in templo ("in the temple") where the Hebrew has "on the wing of abominations."
notes.10:1: Latin fortitudo magna ("great strength") and intelligentia enim est opus in visione ("for understanding is needed in a vision") are distinctive Vulgate renderings of the Hebrew clauses usually taken as "a great conflict" and "he had understanding of the vision." Latin Baltassar is the Latinate form of Daniel's Babylonian name Belteshazzar.
notes.10:11: Latin vir desideriorum ("man of desires") translates literally the Hebrew idiom for a greatly esteemed or beloved man; the same phrase recurs in 10:19.
notes.10:16: Latin dissolutae sunt compages meae ("my joints have been loosened") is a distinctly Vulgate reading corresponding to the Hebrew clause usually rendered "pains/anguish turned upon me."
notes.10:20: Latin Cum ego egrederer, apparuit princeps Graecorum veniens uses past tenses ("When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming"), whereas the Hebrew is normally rendered as future.
notes.11:9: Latin places rex austri in the nominative ("And the king of the south will enter into the kingdom"), making him the subject, whereas the Hebrew is usually read with the king of the north entering the kingdom of the king of the south.
notes.11:30: Latin explicitly renders Hebrew "ships of Kittim" as trieres, et Romani ("triremes and the Romans"), and translates the closing clause as cogitabit adversum eos ("plot against those") rather than "show regard for those."
notes.11:37: Latin et erit in concupiscentiis feminarum ("and he will be given to the desires of women") is an affirmative statement, whereas the Hebrew places "the desire of women" under the surrounding negation.
notes.11:38: Latin transliterates Hebrew ma'uzzim ("fortresses") as the proper name Maozim here and in 11:39; in 11:39 Latin gratuito ("for nothing") also differs from Hebrew "for a price."
notes.11:45: Latin transliterates Hebrew appadno ("his palace/pavilion") as the place name Apadno, and renders the following phrase usque ad summitatem ejus ("even to its summit") rather than "to his end."
notes.12:1: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply "a time will come such as has not been" (et veniet tempus quale non fuit), without the qualifier "of distress" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.12:2: The Vulgate renders the rare Hebrew word dera'on ("abhorrence/contempt") as ut videant semper ("so that they may always see"), reflecting Jerome's derivation of the term from the Hebrew root for "seeing."
notes.12:6: The Vulgate reads first-person Et dixi ("And I said"), making Daniel the questioner, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads third-person "and he/one said."
notes.12:7: Latin dispersio manus populi sancti ("the scattering of the hand of the holy people") literally reproduces the Hebrew idiom "hand" for power or strength, though Latin manus can also denote a "band" or "company."
notes.12:10: The Vulgate translates Hebrew yitbararu as Eligentur ("will be chosen," taking the root in the sense "select" rather than "purify") and reads quasi ignis probabuntur ("tested like fire," nominative ignis) where the Hebrew has "will be refined."

unplaced.text: Susanna groaned and said, "Distress surrounds me on every side; for if I do this, it is death for me, yet if I do not do it, I will not escape your hands."
"But it is better for me to fall into your hands without doing this deed than to sin in the sight of the Lord."
And the king said to Daniel, "Look, now you cannot say that this one is not a living god; so worship him."
And Daniel said, "I worship the Lord my God, because He Himself is the living God; but this one is not a living god."
"As for you, king, give me authority, and I will kill the dragon without sword or club." And the king said, "I give it to you."

So Daniel took pitch, fat, and hair, and boiled them together; he made them into lumps and put them into the dragon's mouth, and the dragon burst open. And he said, "Look at the one you were worshiping."
And when the people had come to her husband Joakim, the two elders also came, full of wicked intent against Susanna, in order to put her to death.
And they said before the people, "Send for Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, wife of Joakim." And immediately they sent for her.
And she came with her parents, her children, and all her relatives.
Now Susanna was very delicate and beautiful in appearance.
But those wicked men ordered that she be unveiled (for she was veiled), so that at least in this way they might take their fill of her beauty.
So her own people and all who knew her were weeping.
Then the two elders stood up in the middle of the people and placed their hands on her head.
Weeping, she looked up to heaven, for her heart had confidence in the Lord.
And the elders said, "While we were walking alone in the orchard, this woman came in with two young women, closed the doors of the orchard, and sent the young women away from her."
"Then a young man who had been hiding came to her and lay with her."
"Now while we were in a corner of the orchard, seeing the wickedness, we ran to them and saw them having intercourse together."
"And as for him, we were unable to catch him, because he was stronger than we were, and after opening the doors he leaped out."
"But when we seized this woman, we asked who the young man was, and she refused to tell us. We are witnesses to this matter."
The crowd believed them as elders and judges of the people, and they condemned her to death.
As for those who had been the cause of his destruction, he threw them into the den, and they were devoured in an instant before him.
And the Lord heard her voice.
Standing in the middle of them, he said, "Are you so foolish, sons of Israel, that without judging or learning what is true, you have condemned a daughter of Israel?"
And Daniel said to them, "Separate them far from one another, and I will judge them."
So when they had been separated from one another, he called one of them and said to him, "You who have grown old in evil days, now your sins that you committed before have come upon you."
"Passing unjust judgments, oppressing the innocent, and releasing the guilty, though the Lord says, 'You must not kill the innocent and the righteous.'"
"Now then, if you saw her, say under what tree you saw them conversing with one another." And he said, "Under a mastic tree."
Then Daniel said, "Very well, you have lied against your own head; for look, the angel of God, having received the sentence from Him, will split you in two."
unplaced.note: In Latin, Daniel plays on the sound of schino ("mastic tree") in the preceding verse and scindet ("will split").

unplaced.text: And once he was removed, he ordered the other one to come and said to him, "Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you, and lust has perverted your heart."
"This is how you used to treat the daughters of Israel, and out of fear they spoke with you; but a daughter of Judah did not tolerate your wickedness."
unplaced.note: The Latin phrase "spoke with you" (loquebantur vobis) is used here as a euphemism for intimate relations.

unplaced.text: "Now then, tell me under what tree you caught them talking with one another." And he said, "Under a holm oak."
Then Daniel said to him, "Very well, you too have lied against your own head; for the angel of the Lord is waiting, holding a sword, to cut you in two and put both of you to death."
unplaced.note: Daniel's verdict ("cut you in two," Latin secet) reflects the wordplay on prino ("holm oak") in the preceding verse.

unplaced.text: Then the entire assembly cried out with a loud voice and blessed God, who saves those who hope in Him.
And a decree was issued by me that all the wise men of Babylon be brought into my presence, and that they make the explanation of the dream known to me.

Belteshazzar, chief of the diviners, since I know that you have the spirit of the holy gods in you, and no mystery is impossible for you, relate the visions of my dreams, which I saw, and their explanation.
unplaced.note: The Vulgate uses Baltassar for both Daniel's Babylonian name (Belteshazzar) and the king in chapter five (Belshazzar).

unplaced.text: I have heard about you that you have the spirit of the gods, and that greater knowledge, understanding, and wisdom have been found in you.
And now the wise men, the magicians, have come into my presence to read this writing and make its interpretation known to me; and they were unable to declare the meaning of this message.
King, the Most High God gave a kingdom and majesty, glory and honor to your father Nebuchadnezzar.

And because of the majesty that He had given him, all peoples, tribes, and languages trembled and feared him: those whom he wished, he put to death; and those whom he wished, he struck; and those whom he wished, he exalted; and those whom he wished, he humbled.
unplaced.note: The Vulgate reads percutiebat ("he struck"), where the Aramaic text has "he kept alive."

unplaced.text: But when his heart was lifted up, and his spirit was hardened into pride, he was deposed from the throne of his kingdom, and his glory was taken away;

and he was cast out from the sons of men, and even his heart was placed with the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys; he also ate grass like an ox, and his body was soaked with the dew of heaven, until he came to know that the Most High has authority in the kingdom of men and will raise up over it whomever He wills.
unplaced.note: The Vulgate literally reads "his heart was placed with the beasts" (cor ejus cum bestiis positum est).
